title: Chapter 4 — The Principle Of The Sovereignty Of The People In America
paragraphs: Whenever we discuss the political laws of the United States, we must begin with the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people. This principle, which lies more or less at the bottom of almost all human institutions, generally stays out of sight. It is obeyed without being acknowledged, or if it is brought to light for a moment, it is quickly cast back into the gloom of the sanctuary. “The will of the nation” is one of those phrases that the cunning and the despotic of every age have abused most freely. Some have seen it in the bought votes of a few hangers-on of power; others in the votes of a timid or self-interested minority; still others have found it in a people’s silence, assuming that the fact of submission established the right to command.

In America the principle of the sovereignty of the people is neither barren nor concealed, as it is in some other nations. It is recognized by custom and proclaimed by law; it spreads freely and reaches its most remote consequences without obstruction. If there is any country in the world where the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people can be fairly appreciated, where it can be studied in its application to society, and where its dangers and advantages can be foreseen, that country is America.

I have already observed that from the beginning, the sovereignty of the people was the fundamental principle in most of the British colonies in America. Back then, however, it was far from exerting the influence over the government that it exercises today. Two obstacles, one external and one internal, held back its advance. It could not openly disclose itself in the laws of colonies still required to obey the mother country. It was therefore forced to spread secretly, gaining ground in the provincial assemblies and especially in the townships.

American society was not yet ready to embrace it with all its consequences. The intelligence of New England and the wealth of the country south of the Hudson (as I showed in the previous chapter) long exercised a kind of aristocratic influence, which tended to keep social authority in the hands of a few. Public officials were not all elected, and not all citizens could vote. The electoral franchise was everywhere subject to certain limits and tied to a property qualification — very low in the North, more substantial in the South.

Then the American Revolution broke out, and the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people, which had been nurtured in the townships and municipalities, took possession of the State. Every class rallied to its cause; battles were fought and victories won for it, until it became the law of laws.
A change no less rapid took place within society itself, where the law of inheritance completed the abolition of local influences.

At the very moment when this consequence of the laws and of the Revolution became visible to every eye, victory was irrevocably declared in favor of the democratic cause. All power was in fact in its hands, and resistance was no longer possible. The upper classes submitted without a murmur and without a struggle to an evil that had become inevitable. The usual fate of falling powers awaited them: each of their members pursued his own interests, and since it was impossible to wrest power from a people they did not hate enough to defy, their only goal was to secure its goodwill at any price. The most democratic laws were therefore voted in by the very men whose interests they damaged. And so, although the higher classes did not provoke popular hostility against themselves, they accelerated the triumph of the new order — so that by a strange reversal, the democratic impulse proved most irresistible in the very States where aristocracy had held the firmest grip. Maryland, which had been founded by men of rank, was the first to proclaim universal suffrage and to introduce the most democratic forms into its government.

When a nation lowers the voting qualification, it can easily be foreseen that sooner or later it will be abolished altogether. There is no rule more constant in the history of society: the more voting rights are extended, the greater the need to extend them further. After each concession, democracy grows stronger, and its demands grow with its strength. The ambition of those below the threshold is stirred in exact proportion to the number of those above it. The exception eventually becomes the rule, concession follows concession, and nothing short of universal suffrage can bring the movement to a halt.

Today the principle of the sovereignty of the people has developed, in the United States, as fully in practice as the imagination can conceive. It is unencumbered by the fictions that have been thrown over it in other countries, and it takes every possible form according to the needs of the moment. Sometimes the laws are made by the people as a body, as in Athens; at other times its representatives, chosen by universal suffrage, conduct business in its name and almost under its direct control.

In some countries there exists a power that, while partly foreign to the social body, directs it and forces it along a certain course. In others the governing force is divided, lying partly within and partly outside the ranks of the people. But nothing of the kind is to be found in the United States. There, society governs itself for itself. All power is gathered at its center, and you will scarcely meet an individual who would dare to conceive, much less express, the idea of seeking power elsewhere. The nation takes part in making its laws by choosing its legislators, and in executing them by choosing the agents of the executive branch. It may almost be said to govern itself, so feeble and so narrow is the share left to the administration, and so little do the authorities forget their popular origin and the power from which they are derived. *a [Footnote a: See Appendix, H.]
